title: The Bottleneck in a Fab Isn't the Lithography Machine—It's the OHT Robots on the Ceiling
dek: The real capacity constraint in a wafer fab isn't just the lithography machine; it's also the OHT vehicles scurrying along the ceiling. The 300mm transition made them indispensable, and today the market is a duopoly of Daifuku and Muratec.
why: The rarely discussed AMHS segment covers floor costs, injury data, and a Daifuku/Muratec duopoly—a missing piece beyond the lithography narrative.
who: Fab manufacturing and automation engineers, semiconductor equipment investors, and anyone wanting to understand hidden costs in advanced-node capacity stories.
skip: Daifuku's pre-WWII history can be fast-forwarded; jump straight to the industry consolidation conclusion at 18:38.

points.h: Fab transport problems are baked into the bay layout
points.body: Fabs are divided into sub-areas by processing zone, and within each zone, tools are arranged in bays. Movement within a bay is called intrabay; movement between bays is interbay. Each bay has stockers—automated parking towers that hold roughly 150–250 FOUPs. Stockers replaced open shelving, saving cleanroom floor space, helping track work-in-progress, and serving as buffers and zone entry/exit points. The entire transport problem grows out of this layout.

points.h: Cleanroom floors are too expensive, so transport went to the ceiling
points.body: Once a wafer leaves a tool, it must be sealed in a FOUP; dust would ruin it. Early on, people pushed FOUPs across bays, but a single lot could be worth $100,000, so automation began in the 1980s. First came floor-level AGVs, limited to about 1 ft/s for safety; then rail-guided RGVs were faster but took up floor space and needed guarding. PRI's Aerotrak hung a monorail from the ceiling, and by 1988 such interbay AMHS was common. Cleanroom floors are expensive, so this move was inevitable.

points.h: After interbay automation, humans became the new bottleneck
points.body: Once interbay was automated, the bottleneck shifted to operators manually moving FOUPs from stockers to tools. A skilled operator takes 30–90 seconds per load change, but a bay has many tools. The author recalls a DRAM fab where buzzers rang constantly—tools waiting for operators. Intrabay automation must sense tool processing status and load/unload automatically; any misalignment or timing error stops the tool. In the early days there were no industry standards, so each company invented its own. Hot lots and SUPER hot lots, being awkward to program, were often still carried by operators at a run.

points.h: 300mm wasn't an upgrade—it was an ultimatum for automation
points.body: The shift to 300mm wafers in the late 1990s made manual handling unsustainable. SEMATECH found that 15–20% of tool time in older fabs was wasted waiting for operators or FOUPs; tools were more expensive, heavier, and took more floor space. A loaded 300mm FOUP weighs about 9 kg, exceeding the 'maximum acceptable weight' for repetitive lifting in ergonomics. A Taiwanese 200mm fab survey found 40–60% of workers had shoulder discomfort and 30–50% had back problems. A high-volume 300mm bay needs over 300 moves per hour, versus 125–175 in older fabs—automation was the only option.

points.h: OHT won by not using floor space, not by being faster
points.body: The core of second-generation AMHS is the OHT: vehicles run on ceiling rails, stop directly above a tool, and use a hoist to pick/place FOUPs at the tool's front-end interface—a few seconds per move, up to 60 m/min. It doesn't take floor space or compete with people, but it's expensive to install, routes are inflexible, and hanging over tools poses a particle risk. To address this, SEMI defined common standards for loadport configuration and optical signal exchange between vehicle and tool, ensuring handoffs succeed and saving cost. OHT became the only choice for a unified system.

points.h: A full system costs over $100 million, so most fabs kept using people
points.body: TSMC was one of the first to open a 300mm fab with full ceiling AMHS: Fab 12 in Hsinchu, initially running 150nm then moving to 130nm, with 2,000 vehicles making 600,000 moves per day. But the scale and cost are daunting—a complete 300mm interbay/intrabay system runs $50–100 million and takes two years to install. For years after, many fabs still relied on manual wafer handling. Automation wasn't a one-time switch.

points.h: AMHS scheduling has no optimal solution, only trade-offs
points.body: Scheduling is done centrally by the fab's control system: assigning vehicles, planning routes, handling congestion, and avoiding deadlocks and down tools. Fabs don't add vehicles for peak demand; they work with what they have. Hot lots and rework must be written as special rules. The author's verdict: there is no optimal algorithm. So operators use simulation to optimize targets like average delivery time, on-time delivery, cycle time, or throughput. It's like designing a traffic system for the entire fab.

points.h: The 300mm transition reshuffled the OHT supplier landscape
points.body: Daifuku (大福) is the largest OHT supplier. It started in steel forging machinery, renamed after WWII to avoid zaibatsu dissolution—the name comes from the first characters of its Osaka and Fukuchiyama plants. The turning point was a license for Jervis B Webb chain conveyors, leading to a 1959 supply deal for Toyota's Motomachi plant, and growth alongside Japan's automakers. The 300mm transition reset the market: PRI, struggling with Aeroloader R&D costs, was sold to Brooks Automation for $500 million; eventually Daifuku and Muratec consolidated the industry and have dominated ever since.

terms.def: The collective automated equipment in a fab for moving FOUPs, including AGVs, OHTs, and stockers.
Standard wafer container, typically holding 25 wafers, used for safe transport between tools.
A vehicle that runs on ceiling rails and uses a hoist to pick/place FOUPs at a tool's front-end interface.
An automated storage/retrieval machine, like an automated parking tower, for buffering wafers and serving as zone entry/exit.
Interbay is transport between bays; intrabay is transport between tools within the same bay.

quotes.text: The first things you will notice upon stepping inside a fab clean room are the equipment. Massive, inscrutable, expensive. But the second things you will notice are the little vehicles puttering around on the ceiling above your head.
I was told that it was because the tool wants to let the operator know that it needs its diaper, sorry wafers, changed.
They even have SUPER hot lots which represent the absolute first priority for every tool and operator on the line.
A study done by SEMATECH in the mid-1990s discovered that in older fabs, 15-20% of tool time is wasted waiting for an operator or FOUP to arrive.

The OHT vehicle aligns itself above the tool. And then it lowers a hoist to either pick up or drop off the FOUP right from the tool's frontend interface. It is magnificent to watch and just takes a few seconds.
In the end, Daifuku and Muratec consolidated the industry between themselves and they dominate it to this day.
